claims.text: Adding a few atomic percent aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy will cause in situ formation of an ordered B2-type precipitate.
The B2-type precipitate will be stable under the proposed operating conditions.
The ordered B2-type precipitate will improve high-temperature mechanical performance by impeding dislocation motion.
Adding aluminum will reduce the alloy's overall density.
A few atomic percent aluminum can preserve the alloy's room-temperature mechanical properties.
The proposed intervention is the addition of a few atomic percent aluminum to an initially aluminum-free refractory high-entropy alloy.
Jet-turbine-relevant high-temperature mechanical loading is approximately 1000–1200 °C.
Partial replacement of heavier refractory elements by aluminum lowers overall alloy density.
Aluminum promotes precipitation of ordered phases in the proposed refractory alloy.
The ordered precipitates act as pinning sites for dislocations during high-temperature deformation.
Dislocation pinning by the precipitates will enhance high-temperature yield strength.
The aluminum-modified alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than an identically processed aluminum-free baseline.
The aluminum-modified alloy will have slightly lower density than the baseline.
The aluminum-modified alloy will retain room-temperature mechanical properties comparable to the baseline.
The proposed effects will hold under mechanical loading at temperatures up to approximately 1200 °C.
Excessive aluminum addition could form brittle or excessive intermetallic phases that degrade room-temperature performance.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as adding aluminum, whereas the density mechanism requires partial replacement of heavy refractory elements. The formulation does not specify whether aluminum is substituted for a particular element or simply added and the composition renormalized.
